lineas.texto: Extract one. You hear two people talking about a book group.
We have not read a book since March and everybody is considerably happier, which I think tells you something.
So what do you actually do when you meet?
We meet. That was always the point and none of us would say it out loud. Somebody was getting through four hundred pages a month out of duty and then apologising for not finishing.
Would you ever go back to the books?

Only if somebody genuinely wanted to, and that is the test we should have applied at the start. A group that meets because it wants to read is a book group. Ours was a way of seeing each other on a Tuesday that needed a reason attached to it.
Extract two. You hear a woman talking about giving up her allotment.
Everybody assumes I gave it up because of my back.
And that was not the reason?

The back was the excuse I used, because it ends the conversation politely. The truth is I had nine years of it and perhaps three of those were any good. The rest was arriving on a Saturday to find out what had died during the week.
It is not bleak, it is honest. And what I miss is not the growing at all. It is the man on the next plot, who talked to me every week for nine years and whose surname I never once learned.
Extract three. You hear two colleagues discussing a new reporting system.
It went live on Monday and I have now entered the same figures three times.
You will enter them three times for about six weeks, and then somebody will quietly build a spreadsheet, and by Christmas we will all be using the spreadsheet.

It is not cynicism, it is the fourth time I have watched it happen. The system is not badly built. It was specified by people who wanted a report, and nobody asked what the report was for. So it collects everything, because everything is safer than choosing.
Are you going to say that at the review?
I will say it, and it will be written down, and the review is in November, and the specification was signed in March.
